questions.q: Harshavardhana ruled from one capital, and his dynasty had an earlier capital elsewhere. Which pair is correct?
questions.a: Harsha ruled from Kannauj; the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty's earlier capital was Sthaneshvara, present-day Thanesar in Haryana. The other pairs reverse the two cities or bring in Ujjayini and Prayaga.
o: Kannauj, with Sthaneshvara as the earlier capital
Sthaneshvara, with Kannauj as the earlier capital
Kannauj, with Ujjayini as the earlier capital
Prayaga, with Sthaneshvara as the earlier capital

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the chapter about Xuanzang?
questions.a: The chapter says he came to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers; it never says he came as an ambassador to sign a trade treaty. The other three statements are in the chapter.
o: He came as an ambassador to sign a trade treaty for China
He travelled around the subcontinent between 630 and 644
He took more than 600 Buddhist manuscripts back to China
He recorded politics, diplomacy, culture and religion

questions.q: Why do historians read Harsha's three Sanskrit plays even though they are only 'stories'?
questions.a: The chapter says historians extract details of governance, social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing from such literature. It does not say the plays give his battle record, his tax lists or a foreigner's view.
o: They reveal details of governance, society, food and clothing
They give the exact boundaries of his empire in each year
They were written by a Chinese pilgrim who visited his court
They list the taxes he collected from every village

questions.q: At a museum, Tanvi reads a label beside a copper plate in Nagari script: 'By my own hand, the great king of kings, Shri Harsha'. What kind of source is she looking at?
questions.a: A copper plate inscription carrying the king's own signature, found at Banskhera. The travelogue, the court biography and the coin are other kinds of source named in the chapter.
o: A copper plate inscription carrying the king's own signature
A travelogue kept by a visiting Chinese pilgrim
A biography of the king written by a poet he patronised
A coin with a peacock fanning its tail on the back

questions.q: Rohan marks on a timeline the point where Harsha's march beyond the Narmada was stopped. Whose power, according to the chapter, held Harsha in check there?
questions.a: Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty held Harsha in check. Narasimhavarman I of the Pallavas later defeated Pulakeshin II, which is why that option tempts; Dharmapala and Dantidurga belong to other dynasties and other regions.
o: Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty
Narasimhavarman I of the Pallava dynasty

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harshavardhana.
1. His rule at Kannauj began in 606 CE.
2. Xuanzang described him as a ruler who stayed away from wars and kept only a small army.
3. Inscriptions show him as a devotee of Shiva, while other sources show him deeply attached to Buddhism.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Xuanzang described a just and energetic ruler who maintained a vast army and was often engaged in military campaigns.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Xuanzang's travelogue is a major source of information for historians of Harsha's period.
Reason (R): Xuanzang took more than 600 Buddhist manuscripts back to China.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. A holds because he left a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. The 600 manuscripts are a separate fact about his purpose, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kadambari  2. Harshacharita  3. Prayaga assembly  4. Varman dynasty of Kamarupa
Column B: a. an ally of Harsha in present-day Assam  b. held every five years, where much wealth was given away  c. a biography of Harsha  d. a novel completed by the author's son
questions.a: Kadambari is the novel that Bana left unfinished (d); Harshacharita is the biography (c); the Prayaga assembly was every five years (b); the Varmans of Kamarupa were allies (a). The distractors swap the novel with the biography or the assembly with the alliance.

questions.q: (a) For how many years did Xuanzang's travels in India last, going by the years the chapter gives? (b) If his 600 manuscripts were carried by 20 horses, what was the average number of manuscripts per horse?
questions.a: (a) 644 - 630 = 14 years. (b) 600 / 20 = 30 manuscripts per horse on average (the book says 'more than 600', so a little more than 30).
s: Part (a): 14 years from 630 to 644
Part (b): 600 divided by 20 gives 30 per horse

questions.q: (a) What kinds of stories do Harsha's three plays weave? (b) Why does the chapter still call them useful for a historian?
questions.a: (a) Love stories with courtly life, and themes of sacrifice and other high ethical values. (b) Historians extract details of culture and society from them: systems of governance, social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing.
s: Part (a): love stories with courtly life, and sacrifice or high ethical values
Part (b): historians extract details of governance, society, technologies, foods and clothing

questions.q: Differentiate between Kadambari and Harshacharita.
questions.a: Kadambari is a complex 7th-century love story across births, dreams and divine worlds, one of the world's first novels. Harshacharita is Bana's biography of Harsha.
s: Kadambari identified as the novel with its love-story plot
Harshacharita identified as the biography of Harsha

questions.q: What happened at Prayaga every five years under Harsha? Name three groups who received what was given.
questions.a: After performing sacred rites, Harsha gave away much wealth at an assembly there. It was offered to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor.
s: Gave away much wealth at an assembly after sacred rites, every five years
Names Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor as recipients

questions.q: Sthaneshvara and Kannauj are both linked with Harsha's dynasty. Differentiate between them.
questions.a: Sthaneshvara (present-day Thanesar in Haryana) was the earlier capital of the Pushyabhuti dynasty. Kannauj (Kanyakubja, by the River Ganga in Uttar Pradesh) was where Harsha ascended the throne in 606 CE and ruled.
s: Sthaneshvara as the earlier capital in present-day Haryana
Kannauj as the city on the Ganga where Harsha ruled from 606 CE

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Harsha signed as maharajadhiraja, the great king of kings, so his empire must have covered the whole subcontinent.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. A title in a signature does not prove the extent of an empire. The chapter says that its precise extent is not known with certainty, that Pulakeshin II held Harsha in check beyond the Narmada, and that he achieved only mixed success in uniting northern India.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since a title does not prove how far the empire reached
Cites that the extent is not known with certainty or that Pulakeshin II stopped him at the Narmada
Cites mixed success or continuing conflicts with neighbours in the north

questions.q: The chapter says Harsha 'achieved only mixed success' in uniting northern India. Support this with one success and two limits.
questions.a: Success: he expanded his empire over large parts of northern and eastern India and allied with the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa. Limits: Pulakeshin II held him in check beyond the Narmada; conflicts with neighbouring kingdoms continued; the Tripartite Struggle began soon after his death in 647.
s: One valid success (expansion over north and east, or the Varman alliance)
First limit stated correctly
Second limit stated correctly and different from the first

questions.q: Write three clues for a quiz so that the answer is 'Xuanzang'. One clue must carry a number, and each clue must use a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct clues, e.g. a Chinese pilgrim; he travelled in India between 630 and 644; he carried more than 600 manuscripts on 20 horses; Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj in his honour.
s: Clue 1 is correct and from the chapter
Clue 2 is correct and carries a number
Clue 3 is correct, new, and the clues together point to him alone

questions.q: 'Xuanzang's travelogue is a major source of information for historians of this period.' Justify this statement using his purpose, his journey, what he took back and what he recorded.
questions.a: He was a Chinese pilgrim who came, like Faxian before him, to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers. He travelled in the subcontinent between 630 and 644 and took back more than 600 Sanskrit manuscripts on 20 horses to translate into Chinese. He kept a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion in the kingdoms he crossed, including a picture of Kannauj as prosperous and Harsha as just and energetic. An eyewitness record of this kind is therefore a major source.
s: States his purpose: Buddhist sites and Indian teachers
Gives the dates 630 to 644 of the journey
Mentions the 600 manuscripts taken to China
Lists what he recorded: politics, diplomacy, culture, religion
Uses one detail on Harsha or Kannauj to show the value of the account

questions.q: Compare the assembly at Kannauj with the assembly at Prayaga under Harsha, and analyse what the two together show about him.
questions.a: The Kannauj assembly was held in honour of Xuanzang and was attended by kings and leaders of many religious sects. The Prayaga assembly, at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, was held every five years; after sacred rites Harsha gave away much wealth to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor. Together they show a king who honoured a foreign scholar, welcomed many beliefs and shared his wealth widely.
s: Purpose and guests of the Kannauj assembly
Frequency and setting of the Prayaga assembly
Recipients at Prayaga
A difference or similarity drawn between the two
Analysis: respect for many beliefs and generosity

questions.q:
The history club of a Pune school drafts a poster. It reads: 'A Chinese traveller came to India in 630 and left in 644. He came to trade silk. Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj for him and gave away riches at Prayaga every year.' The teacher asks the club to check the poster against the chapter.
(a) Find the two statements on the poster that the chapter does not support, and correct them.
(b) A visitor stays exactly in India from 630 to 644, both years included. At most how many five-yearly Prayaga assemblies could fall in these years?
(c) Name the kind of source the traveller's own writing is, and two things it recorded.
(d) The club can print only one headline: 'A Chinese Eye on Harsha's Court' or 'The King Who Gave Away His Wealth'. Choose one and justify it with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) Not to trade silk, but to visit Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers; and the Prayaga assembly was every five years, not every year. (b) At most 3 (for example 630, 635, 640), since a fourth would need 645. (c) A travelogue; it recorded politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the first draws on the travelogue and Kannauj assembly, the second on the five-yearly giving to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor.
s: Part (a): corrects the trade motive and the yearly Prayaga claim
Part (b): at most 3 assemblies, with the working
Part (c): travelogue, with two things it recorded
Part (d): picks a headline and backs it with chapter evidence

questions.q:
A teacher reads this passage aloud. 'The 7th-century novel has a very elaborate and complex plot. It tells of a love story between a prince from Ujjayini and a celestial being. Their romance runs across different births, dreams and divine worlds, with a story often told within another story. On the way, we get glimpses of courtly life, philosophy, nature and aesthetics. The author died before completing it.'
(a) Name the novel and its author, and say who completed it.
(b) Name the other work by the same author and say whom it is about.
(c) Why can a historian use such a novel, or Harsha's plays, as a source?
(d) For a project on courtly life in Harsha's time, would you choose the novel or Xuanzang's travelogue as your main source? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Kadambari by Banabhatta (Bana); his son completed it. (b) Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha. (c) Historians extract details of culture and society, such as governance, social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing, from literature. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the novel offers glimpses of courtly life, philosophy, nature and aesthetics; the travelogue gives an eyewitness account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion, but by an outsider.
s: Part (a): Kadambari, Bana, completed by his son
Part (b): Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha
Part (c): historians draw details of society and culture from literature
Part (d): chooses one source and justifies with its strengths and limits

questions.q: Which three powers fought the 'Tripartite Struggle' over Kannauj?
questions.a: The Palas from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan. The Pallavas are a southern dynasty and the Chalukyas and Cholas were not parties to this struggle.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of Vikramashila?
questions.a: Admission was highly selective: each college had a dvarapandita who tested students before allowing them in. It was not open to every applicant. The other statements are in the chapter.
o: Every applicant was admitted without any test
It was known for its ties with Tibet
It had six colleges and a vast library
It was founded by Dharmapala on the banks of the Ganga

questions.q: Why did the people of Bengal choose Gopala as their king in 750 CE?
questions.a: According to an inscription, Bengal had fallen into disorder after Harsha's death, and Gopala was chosen to restore stability. He then became the first Pala king.
o: To restore stability after a period of disorder
To lead an army into the Tripartite Struggle
To build the monasteries at Vikramashila
To protect the east coast ports from invasion

questions.q: Sneha's cousin in Dhaka says that one of the great Pala monasteries stands in her own country today. Which one is she talking about?
questions.a: Somapura, in present-day Bangladesh. Vikramashila is in present-day Bihar, Nalanda is another monastery the Palas patronised, and Mamallapuram is a Pallava port, not a Pala monastery.

questions.q: Arjun reaches the gate of one college of Vikramashila. A scholar questions him on grammar and logic before letting him in. What role is the scholar playing?
questions.a: He is a dvarapandita, the 'scholar gatekeeper' who tested students, which made admission highly selective. A samanta is a subordinate ruler, not a university official.
o: A dvarapandita who tests every applicant at the gate
A samanta who rules the area for the king
A royal accountant who collects the fees
A village headman who keeps local records

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Palas and the Tripartite Struggle.
1. The Palas won the Tripartite Struggle decisively and held Kannauj for ever.
2. Dharmapala was a great patron of Mahayana Buddhism.
3. The Pala Empire prospered through internal trade and through maritime trade from its east coast seaports.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the struggle was long and indecisive, with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Several successors of Dharmapala patronised Buddhist institutions and yet were said to be devotees of Shiva.
Reason (R): In ancient India, except perhaps for monks and nuns, people could feel at ease with various belief systems and practise different modes of worship at the same time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. Because belief systems were fluid, a ruler could support Buddhist monasteries while worshipping Shiva.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Gopala  2. Dharmapala  3. Vikramashila  4. Bakhtiyar Khilji
Column B: a. plundered Vikramashila in the 12th century  b. chosen in 750 CE to restore stability in Bengal  c. a university with six colleges and scholar gatekeepers  d. expanded the Pala Empire and founded major monasteries
questions.a: Gopala was chosen in 750 CE (b); Dharmapala expanded the empire and founded monasteries (d); Vikramashila had six colleges with gatekeepers (c); Bakhtiyar Khilji plundered it (a). The distractors swap the two Pala kings or the university with its destroyer.

questions.q: Kavya's friend says, 'Three great powers would never fight for an ordinary town.' Using what the chapter tells us about Harsha's reign, give two reasons why Kannauj was worth fighting for.
questions.a: Harsha ruled from Kannauj from 606 CE, so it was the seat of a powerful king who hosted poets and scholars. Xuanzang described it as a beautiful and prosperous city, and Harsha held an assembly there attended by kings and leaders of many sects.
s: One reason: seat of Harsha's powerful kingdom or a city of scholars
Second reason: beautiful and prosperous city, or the great assembly held there

questions.q: (a) Vikramashila had six colleges and nearly 3,000 scholars. What was the average number of scholars per college? (b) The university was founded in the late 8th century and remained a great centre for more than four centuries. Show that its destruction in the 12th century fits this.
questions.a: (a) 'Nearly 3,000' / 6 = about 500 scholars per college. (b) Late 8th century (around 790) plus 400 or more years takes us to around 1190 or later, which lies in the 12th century.
s: Part (a): nearly 3,000 divided by 6 gives about 500
Part (b): adds more than 400 years to the late 8th century and reaches the 12th century

questions.q: State two reasons why the Pala Empire flourished economically.
questions.a: Brisk internal trade, and maritime trade through its seaports on the east coast, which gave pathways to Southeast Asia.
s: Internal trade named as a reason
Maritime trade through east coast seaports to Southeast Asia

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the large Pala monasteries were, 'in effect, the universities of those times'?
questions.a: They attracted numerous students, sometimes from far away and even from beyond India, and offered organised teaching in many subjects, as Vikramashila did with six colleges and a vast library.
s: Attracted numerous students, some from beyond India
Organised teaching and learning, e.g. colleges and library

questions.q: What was the connection between Vikramashila and Tibet?
questions.a: One of its famous teachers travelled to Tibet and translated Sanskrit works into Tibetan. He played a major role in shaping Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism.
s: A teacher travelled to Tibet and translated Sanskrit works into Tibetan
He shaped Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism

questions.q: Meena says, 'The Pala kings patronised Buddhist institutions, but that does not mean every Pala king followed only Buddhism.' Is she right? Argue from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Dharmapala patronised Mahayana Buddhism and its monasteries, but the chapter notes that belief systems were fluid, that Harsha and the Guptas patronised several schools, and that several of Dharmapala's successors, while still patronising Buddhist institutions, were said to be devotees of Shiva.
s: Verdict: agrees, patronage did not mean following only Buddhism
Belief systems were fluid in ancient India
Successors patronised Buddhist institutions yet were Shiva devotees

questions.q: Describe Vikramashila in three points: its size, how admission worked, and its famous link beyond India.
questions.a: It had six colleges, monasteries, temples, lecture halls and a vast library, with nearly 3,000 scholars. Admission was highly selective because each college's dvarapandita tested students. It was especially known for its ties with Tibet.
s: Size: six colleges, nearly 3,000 scholars
Admission tested by a dvarapandita at each college
Ties with Tibet

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Palas and the Rashtrakutas were already fighting each other for Kannauj in 640 CE.' Show with numbers and dates from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Pala dynasty began when Gopala was chosen in 750, which is 750 - 640 = 110 years after 640. Also Harsha was still ruling from Kannauj in 640 (he died in 647), and the Tripartite Struggle began only after his death, in the 8th and 9th centuries.
s: States that Harsha was alive in 640 and died in 647, and the struggle came after
Calculates 750 - 640 = 110 years before the first Pala king
Concludes that the Palas could not have fought for Kannauj in 640

questions.q: Compare the three parties of the Tripartite Struggle and analyse why the struggle for Kannauj ended without a lasting victor.
questions.a: The Palas came from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan. After Harsha died in 647 Kannauj became the centre of a long struggle among them in the 8th and 9th centuries. The three powers repeatedly warred against each other with fluctuating outcomes. The rival states had comparable military strength, so none could keep Kannauj for long against the other two; there was no lasting victor and the struggle was indecisive.
s: Names the three powers
Gives their directions or regions
Gives the period and the prize, Kannauj
Describes the repeated wars with fluctuating results
Analysis: the rivals had comparable military strength, so no lasting victor

questions.q: 'The Pala Empire left a lasting legacy of strong governance and learning.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: Dharmapala expanded the empire and patronised Mahayana Buddhism by founding Vikramashila and Somapura and continuing to support Nalanda. These monasteries were the universities of the time and drew students from far, even from beyond India. Vikramashila had six colleges and a vast library, tested its applicants and had ties with Tibet. The empire also prospered through internal trade and east coast seaports. Even after its decline, it left a legacy of governance and learning in parts of eastern and northern India.
s: Dharmapala's expansion and patronage
Monasteries named: Vikramashila, Somapura, Nalanda
Students from far away and beyond India
Trade and economic strength behind it
Concludes with the legacy after decline

questions.q:
For a role-play on Vikramashila, a Patna school sets up one gate for each college of the university. Forty-eight Class 7 students act as applicants and are shared equally among the gates; a separate student stands at each gate as the gatekeeper. The teacher wants the numbers to match the chapter.
(a) Name the official the gatekeeper students are acting, and say what he did.
(b) According to the chapter, how many colleges did the university have, and so how many applicants stand at each gate?
(c) The chapter gives a figure for the scholars of the whole university. Using it, find the average number of scholars per college.
(d) The principal says a hard gate test will keep the numbers small, while an easy entry will let in students from far away who cannot take a long test. Which should the school's role-play follow? Decide, using what the chapter says about admission and about who came to study.
questions.a: (a) A dvarapandita, the scholar gatekeeper of a college, who tested students before allowing them in. (b) Six colleges, so 48 / 6 = 8 applicants at each gate (the gatekeepers are extra students). (c) Nearly 3,000 scholars / 6 = about 500 scholars per college. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: a hard test matches the highly selective admission of the real university; easy entry matches the way it attracted numerous students from far away, even beyond India.
s: Part (a): dvarapandita who tested students at the gate
Part (b): six colleges, so 48 divided by 6 gives 8
Part (c): nearly 3,000 scholars divided by 6 gives about 500
Part (d): decision justified with selective admission or students coming from afar

questions.q:
A Kolkata museum prepares a wall panel that begins: 'In 750 CE, after a period of confusion in the region, a leader was picked by the people to bring calm. The ruler who came after him won lands across the east and north, built two new centres of learning and went on helping an older one. Boats leaving the eastern coast kept the treasury full.' The museum can afford only one extra display.
(a) Name the first king and the dynasty he began, and name his successor.
(b) Name the two monasteries the successor founded.
(c) How did the ports on the east coast help the kingdom?
(d) The choice is between a model of a monastery gate scene and a case of goods that sailed to Southeast Asia. Which display better explains why the kingdom lasted for long? Decide, and justify with one fact from the chapter, noting one fact that supports the other display.
questions.a: (a) Gopala, who founded the Pala dynasty; his successor was Dharmapala. (b) Vikramashila (in Bihar) and Somapura (in Bangladesh). (c) They carried brisk maritime trade, giving pathways to Southeast Asia and adding to the empire's wealth. (d) Either display is acceptable if reasoned: the monastery scene rests on the monasteries as universities drawing students from far; the trade case rests on internal and maritime trade that enriched the empire. A fact from the other side must be noted.
s: Part (a): Gopala, Pala dynasty, successor Dharmapala
Part (b): Vikramashila and Somapura
Part (c): maritime trade with Southeast Asia from the east coast
Part (d): display chosen, justified, and a fact from the other side noted

questions.q: Who founded the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty in the mid-8th century?
questions.a: Nagabhata I founded it. Bhoja was its celebrated 9th-century ruler, Dantidurga founded Rashtrakuta independence and Gopala began the Pala dynasty.

questions.q: What does 'Gurjara' in the name of the Gurjara-Pratiharas refer to?
questions.a: A region between Gujarat and Rajasthan, from where the dynasty probably originated. 'Nripatunga' is Amoghavarsha's title and Varaha is the boar avatar of Vishnu.
o: A region between Gujarat and Rajasthan

questions.q: Which statement about the Rashtrakutas is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says they equally patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools of thought. The claim that only Jain scholars were supported is false; the other three are in the chapter.
o: They supported only Jain scholars and refused help to others
They shifted their power centre to present-day Karnataka
Their first independent ruler overthrew the Chalukyas
They encouraged Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada

questions.q: Ritu visits Ellora and is told that the temple in front of her 'is not a construction but a gigantic sculpture' carved out of a hillside. Which king got it made?
questions.a: Krishna I of the Rashtrakutas. Amoghavarsha I is the 64-year ruler, Dantidurga founded the line, and Bhoja belongs to the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

questions.q: A coin collector in Jaipur shows a silver coin about 2 cm across, with Varaha, the boar avatar of Vishnu, on it. The guide says the best-known king of this dynasty even took the name Adi Varaha. Which dynasty issued such coins?
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, whose celebrated king Bhoja was a devotee of Vishnu and was also called Adi Varaha. The Palas, Rashtrakutas and Chalukyas are not linked with this coin in the chapter.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Bhoja built an empire stretching from Punjab and Kathiawar in the west to Kannauj in the east.
2. The Gurjara-Pratihara empire was finally eliminated by the Rashtrakutas.
3. Amoghavarsha I, sometimes called a 'Jain king', refused to patronise Hindu temples.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. The Gurjara-Pratiharas were finally eliminated by the Ghaznavids in the early 11th century, although a Rashtrakuta attack destroyed Kannauj. Amoghavarsha I also patronised Hindu temples.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Kailashanatha temple at Ellora is described as a gigantic sculpture and not as a construction.
Reason (R): It is the largest rock-cut temple in India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but being the largest does not explain why it is called a sculpture. The explanation is that it was carved out of a hillside.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each ruler in Column A with his description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Nagabhata I  2. Bhoja  3. Dantidurga  4. Krishna I
Column B: a. first independent Rashtrakuta ruler, who overthrew the Chalukyas  b. founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty  c. had the Kailashanatha temple carved at Ellora  d. a devotee of Vishnu whose empire reached from Punjab to Kannauj
questions.a: Nagabhata I founded the Gurjara-Pratiharas (b), Bhoja built their great empire (d), Dantidurga was the first independent Rashtrakuta (a) and Krishna I got the Ellora temple made (c). Distractors swap founders with the great kings of the same dynasty.

questions.q: (a) How did Dantidurga become the first independent Rashtrakuta ruler? (b) Where did the Rashtrakutas then shift their power, and what was their capital?
questions.a: (a) In the mid-8th century he overthrew the Chalukyas in the Deccan. (b) They shifted to present-day Karnataka, with their capital at Manyakheta (modern Malkheda).
s: Part (a): overthrew the Chalukyas in the Deccan in the mid-8th century
Part (b): present-day Karnataka, capital Manyakheta (Malkheda)

questions.q: (a) A girl is born on the day Amoghavarsha I's reign begins, and his reign lasts the full 64 years. How old is she on the day it ends? (b) What title did he take, and what does it mean?
questions.a: (a) 64 years old, so a whole lifetime passed under one ruler. (b) 'Nripatunga', meaning 'peak of kings'.
s: Part (a): 64 years
Part (b): Nripatunga, peak of kings

questions.q: Show how the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas each came into the story of Kannauj, one point for each dynasty.
questions.a: Under Bhoja the Gurjara-Pratihara empire stretched to Kannauj and controlled most of north India. Rashtrakuta rulers campaigned successfully in north India and briefly occupied Kannauj; later they destroyed it.
s: Pratihara link: Bhoja's empire reached Kannauj
Rashtrakuta link: briefly occupied (and later destroyed) Kannauj

questions.q: The chapter gives Bhoja more than one name besides his own. Name two of them and say what each refers to.
questions.a: 'Mihira', a name of the Sun, and 'Adi Varaha', where Varaha is the avatar of Vishnu in the form of a boar.
s: Mihira, a name of the Sun
Adi Varaha, linked to the boar avatar of Vishnu

questions.q: A guide at Bhinmal in western Rajasthan says the town was the early capital of a dynasty that became famous for protecting the northwest. (a) Name the dynasty and say what it was famed for. (b) To which other place did its capital seem to shift later?
questions.a: (a) The Gurjara-Pratiharas, who gained fame for pushing back Arab invasions into northwest India. (b) Ujjayini (the early capital was Bhillamala, modern Bhinmal).
s: Part (a): Gurjara-Pratiharas, famed for pushing back Arab invasions
Part (b): capital seems to have shifted to Ujjayini

questions.q: Dev says, 'A dynasty that fought many wars could still find the time and money to create great works.' Is he right? Test this claim using the Rashtrakutas.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter warns us not to imagine such kings as constantly at war: the Rashtrakutas campaigned in north India and Amoghavarsha I fought frequent wars, yet Krishna I got the Kailashanatha temple, the largest rock-cut temple in India, carved at Ellora, and Amoghavarsha I ensured peace and prosperity for 64 years and was a poet in Sanskrit and Kannada.
s: Verdict: agrees, wars did not stop great works
Evidence of wars or campaigns in the north
Evidence of building or culture: Kailashanatha temple, or peace and poetry under Amoghavarsha I

questions.q: Explain, in three points, how the fortunes of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire changed from the 9th century to the early 11th century.
questions.a: In the 9th century Bhoja built an empire controlling most of north India. A century later Rashtrakuta rulers destroyed Kannauj, which hastened the disintegration of the empire. It was finally eliminated in the early 11th century by the Ghaznavids.
s: 9th-century peak under Bhoja
Destruction of Kannauj by Rashtrakuta rulers hastened disintegration
Final elimination by the Ghaznavids in the early 11th century

questions.q: A signboard on 'Nrupatunga Road' in Bengaluru needs three lines about the person it is named after. Write three lines, each using a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct facts, e.g. Amoghavarsha I took the title Nripatunga, 'peak of kings'; he reigned for 64 years and kept peace and prosperity despite frequent wars; he was a fine poet in Sanskrit and Kannada; he was drawn to Jainism but also patronised Hindu temples.
s: Line 1 is correct and from the chapter
Line 2 is correct and a different fact
Line 3 is correct and a different fact again

questions.q: Compare the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas under these heads: origin and founder, capital, greatest period, and patronage. Then say which of the two the chapter shows leaving more lasting monuments.
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were founded by Nagabhata I in the mid-8th century, probably from the Gurjara region of western India, with capitals first at Bhillamala and later Ujjayini; under Bhoja they held most of north India. The Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga, who overthrew the Chalukyas, with their capital at Manyakheta in Karnataka, and were dominant for nearly two centuries; they patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools and Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada. The chapter shows the Rashtrakutas leaving the more lasting monument, the Kailashanatha temple at Ellora.
s: Origin and founders of both dynasties
Capitals of both
Greatest period or extent of each
Patronage by the Rashtrakutas (and the Pratihara devotion to Vishnu)
Conclusion naming the Ellora temple as the lasting monument

questions.q: 'Amoghavarsha I was a ruler of peace and culture even though he fought frequent wars.' Justify this statement from the chapter.
questions.a: He fought frequent wars with neighbouring kingdoms, including the dynasties surveyed earlier, yet managed to ensure peace, prosperity and stability within his empire. His reign lasted 64 years. He took the title Nripatunga, 'peak of kings'. He was drawn to Jainism, which is why he is sometimes called a 'Jain king', but he also patronised Hindu temples. He was a fine poet who composed in Sanskrit and Kannada, and a road in Bengaluru is still named after him.
s: Acknowledges the frequent wars
Peace and prosperity for 64 years
Religious patronage: Jainism and Hindu temples
Poet in Sanskrit and Kannada
Lasting memory such as the title or Nrupatunga Road

questions.q:
A Class 7 group visits Ellora in Maharashtra to see a famous temple. The guide says: 'This temple was made for a king of the dynasty that overthrew the Chalukyas in the Deccan.' Later the group's teacher adds that the same dynasty fought many wars and campaigned as far as the north.
(a) Name the temple and the king who got it made.
(b) Name the three traditions and the three languages the dynasty supported.
(c) The chapter's caption calls the temple 'not a construction but a gigantic sculpture' carved out of a hillside. What does this suggest about the wealth and skill the dynasty could command, despite its wars?
(d) A minister argues that the money should have gone to the army instead. Give one point for the minister and one for the king, and say which is stronger.
questions.a: (a) The Kailashanatha temple, got made by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. (b) Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions; Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada. (c) Carving a whole temple out of a hillside as one sculpture needed great resources, labour and skill, so the dynasty could spare both despite its wars; the chapter says such kings found time and resources to create wonders. (d) Minister: the dynasty fought many wars and was dominant for nearly two centuries because of its army; king: the dynasty was not constantly at war and its wonders are what we remember. Either verdict is acceptable if reasoned.
s: Part (a): Kailashanatha temple and Krishna I
Part (b): three traditions and three languages
Part (c): carving a hillside into a temple shows great resources and skill
Part (d): one point each side and a reasoned verdict

questions.q:
A 10th-century Arab historian and traveller from Baghdad wrote about a Deccan ruler: 'His troops and elephants are innumerable. There is none among the rulers of Sindh and Hind who in his territory respects the Muslims as he does. In his kingdom, Islam is honoured and protected, and mosques, which are always full, have been built for them.' He was writing about a ruler of the dynasty that had earlier overthrown the Chalukyas.
(a) Name the dynasty.
(b) Name the ruler of this dynasty, known for 64 years of peace and prosperity, who also wrote poetry, and give the title he took.
(c) Which other fact from the chapter about this dynasty fits with the traveller's account?
(d) A historian says this passage alone is enough to describe the dynasty's religious policy. Do you agree? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The Rashtrakutas. (b) Amoghavarsha I, who took the title Nripatunga, 'peak of kings'. (c) The dynasty equally patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools of thought. (d) Not alone: it is one foreigner's praise and may be coloured by his view; it should be checked against other evidence such as the dynasty's own patronage of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions. It is still valuable as an outsider's testimony.
s: Part (a): the Rashtrakutas
Part (b): Amoghavarsha I and the title Nripatunga
Part (c): equal patronage of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools
Part (d): judgement on a single source with a reason

questions.q: What does the title 'Rajatarangini' literally mean?
questions.a: 'The River of Kings'. The other titles are invented look-alikes: 'peak of kings' is the meaning of Nripatunga and 'king of kings' is the title in Harsha's signature.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT named in the chapter as a source for the rulers of Kashmir?
questions.a: The chapter names inscriptions, coins and Kalhana's Rajatarangini. Harshacharita is Bana's biography of Harsha, not a source on Kashmir.

questions.q: Lalitaditya Muktapida, seen as a firm ruler of Kashmir, belonged to which dynasty?
questions.a: The Karkota dynasty. The Pushyabhuti were Harsha's dynasty, the Varmans ruled Kamarupa and the Aulikaras were the rulers who defeated the Huna leaders.

questions.q: Adi Shankaracharya established four mathas. Which set names where they were?
questions.a: Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. The other sets replace one or more of these with cities that the chapter does not name.

questions.q: Pooja reads Kalhana's lines: 'Those who are intent on harassing their subjects perish with their families; fortune waits on the descendants of those who reinstate order where there is chaos.' What does this show about his purpose?
questions.a: He wanted to draw moral lessons from history by highlighting the rulers' ethical values. The chapter does not describe him as a recorder of battle dates, a praiser of artisans or a teacher of advaita; that is Shankaracharya's teaching.
o: To draw moral lessons by judging the rulers' ethical values
To praise the artists and artisans of Kashmir
To record the dates of each battle fought
To explain the teaching that the world is maya

questions.q: On a trip near Srinagar, a guide says an 8th-century teacher once visited the hill above the Jhelum, and that he taught that the world we perceive is maya, an illusion. Whom does the guide mean?
questions.a: Adi Shankaracharya, teacher of advaita vedanta. Abhinavagupta belongs to Kashmir Shaivism, Kalhana is the historian and Lalitaditya is a ruler.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Kalhana says he examined eleven earlier works and consulted inscriptions before writing.
2. Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty is seen as a firm ruler.
3. Shankaracharya established all four of his mathas in the Kashmir valley near Srinagar.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: his four mathas stood at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri, in four different corners of India.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kalhana's Rajatarangini is only a list of kings and has no moral purpose.
Reason (R): Kalhana wanted to highlight the ethical values of rulers, or the lack of them, in order to draw moral lessons from history.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false because Kalhana's purpose was not merely to record history but also to draw moral lessons. R is true, so the correct choice is the one that says A is false and R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: (a) Name Kalhana's work, its language and the century in which he composed it. (b) What did it narrate?
questions.a: (a) The Rajatarangini, an epic poem in Sanskrit, composed in the 12th century. (b) The history of Kashmir's ruling dynasties from their beginnings to his own time.
s: Part (a): Rajatarangini, Sanskrit, 12th century
Part (b): history of Kashmir's dynasties from the beginnings to his own time

questions.q: (a) Which four cities hold the mathas set up by Shankaracharya? (b) The chapter asks why he chose four different corners of India rather than central places. Give one reasoned answer.
questions.a: (a) Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. (b) The chapter poses this as a question and gives no single answer, so any reasoned answer is accepted, e.g. mathas at the four corners could carry his teaching to every region and tie the whole country together as one cultural space.
s: Part (a): the four cities named
Part (b): a reasoned explanation linked to reaching all regions

questions.q: What did Shankaracharya teach about brahman and about the world as we perceive it?
questions.a: That brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness, and that the world as we perceive it is maya, or illusion.
s: Brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness
The perceived world is maya or illusion

questions.q: A monk from Tibet in this period wants to study Buddhist manuscripts and also have a copy of a text painted by a skilled artist. (a) To which region of India would the chapter send him for the manuscripts, and why was it a good choice? (b) Why could he expect to find a manuscript painter there?
questions.a: (a) Kashmir, which was a crucial bridge for Buddhist scholarship: scholars, monks and texts travelled between Kashmir, other parts of northern India, Tibet and Central Asia. (b) Kashmir's artisans, sculptors and manuscript painters were in demand across north India and beyond.
s: Part (a): Kashmir, a bridge for Buddhist scholarship linking Tibet and Central Asia
Part (b): manuscript painters and artisans of Kashmir were in demand

questions.q: Compare Lalitaditya Muktapida and Queen Didda as the Rajatarangini presents them, one point each.
questions.a: Lalitaditya of the Karkota dynasty is seen as a firm ruler. After him Kashmir saw conflicts, and in the late 10th century Didda consolidated power through alliances and by ruthlessly eliminating rivals, including her own grandsons, while also founding towns and building and restoring temples.
s: Lalitaditya: a firm ruler of the Karkota dynasty
Didda: alliances and ruthless elimination of rivals, with towns and temples

questions.q: Zoya says, 'Kashmir lay behind high mountains, so it had little part in the culture of the rest of India.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that despite its mountainous geography Kashmir remained well connected to developments elsewhere. It was a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy and arts, and Abhinavagupta's works influenced all of India. It was also a bridge for Buddhist scholarship and its artisans were in demand across north India.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since Kashmir stayed connected despite the mountains
Learning, philosophy and Abhinavagupta's wide influence
Buddhist bridge or artisans in demand beyond Kashmir

questions.q: Explain three steps Kalhana took, or ideals he set himself, to make his history reliable.
questions.a: He examined eleven earlier works by former scholars. He consulted inscriptions on temple consecrations, royal grants and praise records, along with other written works, to overcome errors. He said a worthy writer should be free from love or hatred, like a judge, when relating facts.
s: Examined eleven earlier works
Consulted inscriptions and other written works to correct errors
Ideal of being free from love or hatred, like a judge

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because he wanted to draw moral lessons from the ethical values of rulers.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and give two examples from the chapter that show this purpose at work.
questions.a: Question: Why did Kalhana describe rulers' conduct in the Rajatarangini? Examples: his lines that those who harass their subjects perish with their families while fortune waits on those who reinstate order; his account of Queen Didda's ruthless elimination of rivals.
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First example from the chapter
Second, different example

questions.q: 'Kalhana's method was careful, but his aim was more than recording facts.' Justify this statement, using his sources, his stated ideals and his purpose.
questions.a: Kalhana, a Kashmiri scholar-poet, wrote the Rajatarangini in Sanskrit in the 12th century. He examined eleven earlier works and consulted inscriptions about temple consecrations, royal grants and praise records, which shows care in checking sources. He said that a worthy writer must be free from love or hatred like a judge. Yet his purpose went beyond records: he highlighted the rulers' ethical values to draw moral lessons, as in his lines that those who harass their subjects perish with their families.
s: Who he was, what he wrote, and when
Eleven earlier works examined
Inscriptions and written works consulted
The ideal of being free from love or hatred
Moral purpose with a quoted example

questions.q: 'Despite its mountains, Kashmir was part of the cultural life of the whole subcontinent.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: The chapter says Kashmir remained well connected to political and cultural developments elsewhere. It was a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy and the arts. The school of Kashmir Shaivism produced scholars like Abhinavagupta, whose works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics had a vast influence across India. It was a crucial bridge for Buddhist scholarship as scholars, monks and texts travelled between Kashmir, other parts of northern India, Tibet and Central Asia. Its artisans, sculptors and manuscript painters were in demand across north India and beyond.
s: Stays connected despite mountains
Sanskrit learning and philosophy
Abhinavagupta and Kashmir Shaivism with wide influence
Bridge for Buddhist scholarship to Tibet and Central Asia
Artisans, sculptors and painters in demand beyond Kashmir

questions.q:
A Class 7 history club reads a line by a 12th-century Kashmiri scholar: 'I went through eleven earlier works, and by studying inscriptions and other writings I got past many difficulties caused by mistakes.' Ananya says his method makes his book reliable. Rohit says his praise and blame of kings makes it biased.
(a) Name the scholar and the book.
(b) Name two kinds of inscriptions he consulted, according to the chapter.
(c) Give one way in which his method resembles the way history is checked today (any reasonable comparison is accepted).
(d) For a school project on Kashmir's rulers, would you rely on his book? Decide and justify, using both Ananya's and Rohit's points.
questions.a: (a) Kalhana and the Rajatarangini. (b) Any two of inscriptions relating to temple consecrations, royal grants and laudatory records. (c) Any reasonable comparison, e.g. he cross-checked many earlier works and inscriptions, as historians compare sources today. (d) A reasoned judgement such as: rely on it, but cross-check, since the method is careful but he also meant to draw moral lessons from rulers' conduct.
s: Part (a): Kalhana, Rajatarangini
Part (b): two kinds of inscriptions
Part (c): cross-checking many sources
Part (d): decision using both students' points

questions.q:
A drama group in a Srinagar school plans a scene about a queen of the late 10th century. The script says she made strategic alliances, founded a few towns, built several temples and restored many more. The scholar who wrote about her adds that she also removed rivals without mercy, even her own grandsons, to keep power.
(a) Name the queen and the scholar's book.
(b) What did that scholar want readers to learn from such accounts?
(c) The chapter calls an earlier Karkota king a firm ruler. Name him, and say how this queen's way of holding power differed from his.
(d) The director must decide whether the queen is shown as a builder or as a ruthless schemer. Pick one and justify, using at least one fact for each side.
questions.a: (a) Queen Didda; Kalhana's Rajatarangini. (b) Moral lessons about the ethical values of rulers, or their lack of them. (c) Lalitaditya Muktapida; the queen held power by alliances and by ruthlessly eliminating rivals, after a period of conflicts, rather than being seen as a firm ruler of a settled dynasty. (d) A reasoned choice: builder rests on founding towns and building and restoring temples; schemer rests on eliminating rivals including her grandsons; a balanced portrayal is also acceptable if both sides are used.
s: Part (a): Didda and the Rajatarangini
Part (b): moral lessons about rulers' ethical values
Part (c): Lalitaditya Muktapida, contrasted with Didda's alliances and elimination of rivals
Part (d): choice justified with facts from both sides

questions.q: Which city was the capital of the Pallava dynasty?
questions.a: Kanchi (Kanchipuram) in Tamil Nadu. Vatapi was the Chalukya capital, Madurai the Pandya capital and Tanjavur the Chola capital.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
questions.a: It was Narasimhavarman I of the Pallavas who defeated Pulakeshin II, not the other way round. The other three statements are in the chapter.
o: Pulakeshin II defeated the Pallavas and captured Kanchi
Narasimhavarman I captured Badami but then retreated
The Tungabhadra became an unwritten boundary between the powers
Narasimhavarman I sent a naval expedition to Sri Lanka

questions.q: Who composed the long Sanskrit inscription on the Meguti temple at Aihole?
questions.a: Ravikirti, the court poet of the Chalukyas. Dandin was a Sanskrit poet hosted by the Pallavas, and the other two are not authors of this inscription.

questions.q: Meera stands before the Jain temple on Meguti Hill and reads that its long inscription praises Pulakeshin II highly. Her teacher says a historian must still cross-check it. Why?
questions.a: The chapter says the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, as some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions. It does not say it is unreadable, late or hostile.
o: It is full of exaggeration that other inscriptions contradict
It was written centuries later by a foreign pilgrim
It is in a script nobody can read today
It praises Harsha and finds fault with Pulakeshin II

questions.q: Archaeologists digging at Mamallapuram find old Chinese, Persian and Roman coins. What does the chapter let us conclude?
questions.a: Mamallapuram was a Pallava seaport in trade with distant lands. The coins do not show conquest, nor that the Pallavas minted foreign money, nor that a visitor left them.
o: It was a seaport linked by trade with distant lands
The Pallavas conquered China, Persia and Rome
The Pallavas minted coins on foreign designs
Chalukya traders from Aihole had brought them home

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
2. Narasimhavarman I was also known as 'Mamalla', which means 'wrestler' or 'warrior'.
3. Mahendravarman I was himself a fine poet who left a satirical Sanskrit play.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are in the chapter, so none of the statements is false.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kanchipuram was an economic hub as well as a cultural centre.
Reason (R): The Pallavas were patrons of Jain, Vaishnavite and Shaivite schools of thought.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. Kanchipuram was a hub because of its trade in spices, textiles, ivory and luxury goods, not because of the Pallava patronage of different faiths, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the right description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Ravikirti  2. Mamalla  3. Dandin  4. Vengi
Column B: a. court poet who praised Pulakeshin II at Aihole  b. title of Narasimhavarman I, meaning wrestler or warrior  c. poet of elaborate Sanskrit poetry hosted by the Pallavas  d. capital of the Eastern Chalukyas
questions.a: Ravikirti praised Pulakeshin II (a); Mamalla was Narasimhavarman I's name (b); Dandin was a Sanskrit poet at the Pallava court (c); Vengi was the Eastern Chalukya capital (d). The distractors swap the two poets, one from each dynasty.

questions.q: (a) Name the two capitals of the Chalukyas of Badami, the earlier one first, using their present-day names. (b) For what is each place famous?
questions.a: (a) Aryapura (Aihole) and then Vatapi (Badami), both in Karnataka. (b) Aihole has over a hundred Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples; Badami is famous for its complex of Hindu and Jain cave temples.
s: Part (a): Aihole as the earlier capital and Badami as the later
Part (b): Aihole's hundred-plus temples of three faiths, and Badami's Hindu and Jain cave temples

questions.q: At a school literary fair in Kanchipuram, a stall displays a satirical Sanskrit play written by a Pallava king. (a) Name the king. (b) Name two languages whose literature the Pallavas promoted.
questions.a: (a) Mahendravarman I, himself a fine poet. (b) Sanskrit and Tamil.
s: Part (a): Mahendravarman I
Part (b): Sanskrit and Tamil

questions.q: What is meant by a 'monolithic' temple? Where did the Pallavas carve such temples?
questions.a: A monolithic temple is made of a single stone or rock. The Pallavas carved rock-cut caves and monolithic temples at Mamallapuram.
s: Monolithic means made of a single stone or rock
Mamallapuram named as the site

questions.q: Differentiate between the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Eastern Chalukyas.
questions.a: The Western Chalukyas were a revival of the dynasty in the west from the 10th century onward, with their capital at Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan in northern Karnataka). The Eastern Chalukyas were an eastern branch that became independent as the Badami empire declined, ruling from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
s: Western Chalukyas: 10th century revival, capital Kalyani
Eastern Chalukyas: branch ruling from Vengi in Andhra Pradesh

questions.q: After defeating Pulakeshin II and capturing Badami, what two things did Narasimhavarman I do?
questions.a: He retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra River as an unwritten boundary between the two powers, and he sent a naval expedition to Sri Lanka to help a Sinhalese prince recover his lost throne.
s: Retreated with the Tungabhadra as an unwritten boundary
Naval expedition to Sri Lanka to help a Sinhalese prince

questions.q: Aarav says, 'Ravikirti's inscription praises Pulakeshin II too highly, so it is useless as evidence.' Is he completely right, partly right or wrong? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, since some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions, so it cannot be trusted blindly. But it is not useless: there is no doubt that in the early 7th century most of India was dominated by Harsha north of the Vindhyas and Pulakeshin II south of them, so some of its content can be accepted after cross-checking.
s: Verdict: partly right, since the inscription needs checking but is not useless
Poetical style and exaggerations contradicted by other inscriptions
Acknowledges that the two imperial powers claim is still accepted

questions.q: Using three facts from the chapter, show that Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram were centres of trade as well as of culture.
questions.a: Kanchipuram traded in spices, textiles including silk, ivory and other luxury goods. The Pallavas had trade relations with Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia through seaports, particularly Mamallapuram. Ancient Chinese, Persian and Roman coins were found there in excavations.
s: Goods traded at Kanchipuram
Trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia via seaports
Foreign coins found at Mamallapuram

questions.q: A student writes, 'By the mid-8th century the Pallavas had replaced the Chalukyas as rulers of the Deccan.' Show from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says that by the mid-8th century it was the Rashtrakutas who replaced the Chalukyas in the Deccan. The Pallavas, after capturing Badami, retreated to keep the Tungabhadra as a boundary, and they themselves were overthrown in the late 9th century by the Chola king Aditya I.
s: States that the Rashtrakutas replaced the Chalukyas
Notes that the Pallavas held Badami only briefly, since they retreated to the Tungabhadra boundary
Pallavas were themselves overthrown by Aditya I in the late 9th century

questions.q: Compare the Chalukyas and the Pallavas under these heads: founder or greatest king, capital, the clash between them, and patronage of religion and literature (for the Chalukyas' literature, use the Eastern Chalukyas).
questions.a: The Chalukyas were founded by Pulakeshin I in the mid-6th century and expanded under his grandson Pulakeshin II, with the capital first at Aryapura and later at Vatapi. The Pallavas, with their capital at Kanchi, peaked under Mahendravarman I and his son Narasimhavarman I. Pulakeshin II was defeated by the Pallavas and Narasimhavarman I captured Badami, though he retreated. Both patronised Hindu, Jain and other schools: the Pallavas promoted Sanskrit and Tamil literature and the Eastern Chalukyas Telugu and Kannada.
s: Founder or greatest king of each
Capitals of each
Their clash and its result
Religious patronage of each
Literary patronage of each

questions.q: 'A historian must read different sources together.' Justify this using the Meguti inscription at Aihole and Xuanzang's remarks on the Chalukya kingdom and on Kanchi.
questions.a: The inscription by Ravikirti praises Pulakeshin II in a highly poetical style and records his victories over Harsha and rival kings, but some facts it presents are contradicted by other inscriptions, so it is exaggerated. Xuanzang, an outsider, wrote that the king's beneficent actions are felt over a great distance and that his subjects obey him with perfect submission. At Kanchi he gave figures of 100 monasteries and 10,000 priests which are likely exaggerated, but also noted 80 Hindu temples, many Jains and the people's attachment to honesty and learning. Each source has strengths and flaws, so they must be read together.
s: The inscription and its exaggerations
Contradiction by other inscriptions
Xuanzang's remark on Pulakeshin II
Xuanzang's figures and remarks on Kanchi
Conclusion: sources have to be read together

questions.q:
A school heritage trail in Karnataka has three hours at Aihole. The trail leader has read that the site was once the earlier capital of a dynasty that later ruled from a place with famous cave temples, and that a long inscription stands on a hill temple there. The leader must plan the visit.
(a) Name the dynasty and give the old name of Aihole.
(b) Name the three traditions whose temples the chapter says stand at Aihole.
(c) At the Meguti temple the group will read a long inscription. Name its poet and the king it praises, and say why the guide warns that it must be cross-checked.
(d) With only three hours, should the group spend the longest time on the inscription or on walking through as many temples as possible? Decide, using what the chapter says each can teach.
questions.a: (a) The Chalukyas; Aryapura (later Ayyavole). (b) Hindu, Buddhist and Jain. (c) Ravikirti, the court poet, praising Pulakeshin II; the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, and some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the inscription teaches about Pulakeshin II's victories, and how a historian tests a source; the temples show the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions side by side at one site.
s: Part (a): Chalukyas and Aryapura
Part (b): Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples
Part (c): Ravikirti, Pulakeshin II, and the exaggeration contradicted elsewhere
Part (d): decision tied to what the inscription or the temples teach

questions.q:
A Chinese pilgrim who visited the Pallava capital in the 7th century counted 100 Buddhist monasteries with 10,000 priests there, besides 80 Hindu temples and many Jains. A textbook adds that these figures are likely exaggerated. About the people he wrote that they are 'deeply attached to the principles of honesty and truth' and 'highly esteem learning'.
(a) Name the pilgrim and the present-day name of the capital.
(b) Name the two Pallava kings, father and son, under whom the dynasty reached its peak.
(c) Which parts of the pilgrim's account would you still accept even if the figures are exaggerated?
(d) A museum wants to use the account on a panel titled 'A City of Many Faiths'. Should it print the numbers? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Xuanzang; Kanchipuram. (b) Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I. (c) That Kanchi had Buddhist monasteries, Hindu temples and many Jains, and that its people valued honesty and learning, since these do not depend on exact counts. (d) A reasoned decision, e.g. print the faiths and the quotation but flag the numbers as likely exaggerated, or leave the numbers out.
s: Part (a): Xuanzang and Kanchipuram
Part (b): Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I
Part (c): the mix of faiths and the character of the people
Part (d): decision about the numbers with a reason

questions.q: The Cholas were 'reborn' in the 9th century. Under whom, and from which new capital?
questions.a: Under Vijayalaya, from his new capital at Tanjavur. Aditya I was his son and the conqueror of the Pallavas; Madurai, Kanchi and Korkai belong to the Pandyas and Pallavas.

questions.q: Which kingdom, also known as the Chera Perumals, kept its independence along the Kerala coast?
questions.a: The Cheras. The Pandyas were in southern Tamil Nadu, the Cholas around the Kaveri delta and the Pallavas around Kanchi.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the Pandyas is NOT in the chapter?
questions.a: Madurai, not Tanjavur, was the Pandya capital. The other statements, about Korkai, the Cholas sweeping them aside and their return, are in the chapter.
o: Their capital was Tanjavur, a vibrant cultural centre
They traded with Southeast Asia through ports like Korkai
The Cholas swept them aside in the 10th century
They re-emerged about three centuries later

questions.q: Which pair of sources mentions the Pandya, Chola and Chera kingdoms nearly a thousand years before this period?
questions.a: An edict of Ashoka, which names them as his southern neighbours, and Sangam literature, the earliest collections of Tamil poetry. The other pairs are sources of later periods or other regions.
o: An edict of Ashoka and Sangam literature

questions.q: A guide in the Thanjavur bronze gallery points to an early Chola Nataraja, 'Lord of dance', and says it shows what the dynasty valued. Which statement from the chapter does the sculpture best support?
questions.a: The Cholas patronised arts such as sculpture and architecture. The Pandyas ruled from Madurai, the Cheras kept the Kerala coast independent, and Aditya I is credited with defeating the Pallavas, not with sculpture.
o: The Cholas patronised sculpture and architecture
The Pandyas ruled the Kaveri delta from Thanjavur
The Cheras built the empire's largest navy
Aditya I made sculpture the Pallavas' chief art

questions.q: Karthik's family farms near Kumbakonam in the Kaveri delta. His teacher asks why the Chola heartland stayed so prosperous. Which reason is in the chapter?
questions.a: The fertile Kaveri delta together with efficient irrigation techniques gave a steady agricultural output. Gold mines, timber from Himalayan forests and annual tribute from the Pallavas are not given as the reason.
o: Fertile delta land and efficient irrigation gave steady crops
Rich gold mines in the Kaveri delta paid for the empire
A trade in timber from the Himalayan forests
Tribute from the Pallavas collected every year

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Madurai, the capital of the Cholas, was a vibrant cultural centre.
2. The Cheras, along the Kerala coast, were conquered and ruled by the Pandyas.
3. Aditya I, son of Vijayalaya, expanded Chola power by defeating the Pallavas.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 3 is correct. Madurai was the Pandya capital and the Cholas ruled from Tanjavur. The Cheras maintained their independence.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chola inscriptions use both Tamil and Sanskrit.
Reason (R): The Cholas promoted only Sanskrit literature.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false because the Cholas promoted Tamil as well as Sanskrit literature, which is exactly why their inscriptions use both languages.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name the capitals of the Pandyas and of the Cholas. (b) Which of the two kingdoms swept the other aside in the 10th century, and after how long did the defeated one re-emerge?
questions.a: (a) Madurai (Pandyas) and Tanjavur (Cholas). (b) The Cholas swept the Pandyas aside; the Pandyas re-emerged some three centuries later.
s: Part (a): Madurai and Tanjavur matched to the right kingdoms
Part (b): Cholas swept aside the Pandyas, who returned after about three centuries

questions.q: Lakshmi reads in a museum that a copper plate mentions a translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil. (a) Which kingdom, with which capital, is the copper plate speaking of? (b) Why can we not read that translation today?
questions.a: (a) The Pandyas, with their capital at Madurai. (b) The chapter says the translation has unfortunately not survived; we know of it only from the copper plate.
s: Part (a): the Pandyas, capital Madurai
Part (b): the translation has not survived

questions.q: Name two features of the Chola empire for which it became known.
questions.a: Any two of: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy, grand temples; also patronage of sculpture and architecture, and of Tamil and Sanskrit literature.
s: First valid feature
Second valid and different feature

questions.q: What evidence shows that the Pandyas traded overseas, and which port is named?
questions.a: Their coins and inscriptions attest to maritime trade with Southeast Asia, through ports such as Korkai.
s: Coins and inscriptions as the evidence, with Southeast Asia
Korkai named as a port

questions.q: Explain how two languages were used in a land grant inscription of this period, and suggest one reason for using two.
questions.a: The ruler and his dynasty were praised in Sanskrit, while the operative details of the grant were recorded in the local language. A reasoned suggestion, e.g. Sanskrit gave the grant prestige while the local language let the people concerned understand it.
s: Sanskrit for praise, local language for operative details
A reasonable explanation for using both

questions.q: Imran says, 'The Cheras kept their independence along the Kerala coast even though their neighbours were militarily powerful.' Is this claim supported by the chapter? Give your evidence.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the Cheras, also known as Chera Perumals, maintained their independence along the Kerala coast despite their neighbours' military power. The neighbours, the Cholas and Pandyas, were often at war with each other, which fits the claim; but the chapter says little more about the Cheras.
s: Verdict: yes, the claim is supported
Cheras kept independence along the Kerala coast
Neighbours were powerful and often at war with each other

questions.q: Compare the Pandyas and the Cholas on three points: where they were strong, how they traded or built, and how their fortunes changed.
questions.a: The Pandyas controlled much of southern Tamil Nadu with Madurai as capital, while the Cholas held the Kaveri delta with Tanjavur as capital. The Pandyas traded with Southeast Asia through Korkai and built rock-cut temples; the Cholas had a powerful navy and grand temples. The Pandyas were swept aside by the Cholas in the 10th century but re-emerged three centuries later, while the Cholas were dominant until the 13th century.
s: Region and capital of each
Trade, navy or building of each
Change in fortunes over the centuries

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because the fertile delta and efficient irrigation ensured a steady agricultural output.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and name two other things for which the dynasty was known.
questions.a: Question: Why did the Chola heartland remain prosperous? Other things: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy and grand temples (any two).
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First other feature of the Chola empire
Second, different feature

questions.q: Compare the Pandyas, the Cheras and the Cholas on capital or region, trade and culture, and fortunes in this period. Then analyse what contributed to the Cholas building the biggest empire.
questions.a: The Pandyas ruled southern Tamil Nadu from Madurai, traded with Southeast Asia through Korkai and patronised poets; the Cholas swept them aside in the 10th century. The Cheras held the Kerala coast and maintained their independence. The Cholas, reborn under Vijayalaya with Tanjavur as capital, expanded under Aditya I, who defeated the Pallavas. The Cholas' empire was helped by (the chapter lists these features and does not say one alone caused it): the fertile Kaveri delta and efficient irrigation, an efficient administration and a strong navy.
s: Pandyas: capital, trade, culture
Cheras: Kerala coast and independence
Cholas: Vijayalaya, Tanjavur, Aditya I
How fortunes differed
Analysis of Chola strengths: agriculture, administration, navy

questions.q: 'The Cholas ended up building one of the largest empires in south Indian history.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: The Cholas were reborn under Vijayalaya in the 9th century with a new capital at Tanjavur. His son Aditya I defeated the Pallavas and brought most of present-day Tamil Nadu and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh under Chola control. They were known for an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy and grand temples, and they patronised sculpture and architecture and promoted Tamil and Sanskrit. The fertile Kaveri delta with efficient irrigation ensured steady agricultural output. Their dominance lasted until the 13th century.
s: Rebirth under Vijayalaya and Tanjavur
Aditya I's conquests
Administration, navy, temples
Arts and languages, and agriculture
Duration of dominance until the 13th century

questions.q:
A museum in Madurai is planning a timeline wall. A volunteer places two cards: 'Pandyas rise to power (6th century)' and 'The Pandyas are swept aside (10th century)'. The director asks her to finish the story.
(a) Which dynasty swept the Pandyas aside, and from which capital did that dynasty rule?
(b) In which century do the Pandyas re-emerge?
(c) Name two features for which the dynasty of part (a) became known.
(d) The wall has room for a large panel on only one of the two dynasties. Which should it be? Decide and justify with the dates from the timeline and your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Cholas, from Tanjavur. (b) The 13th century, about three centuries after the 10th. (c) Any two: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy, grand temples. (d) Either choice is acceptable if justified: the Pandyas rose by the 6th century, were swept aside in the 10th and re-emerged in the 13th, a story of return; the Cholas were dominant until the 13th century with their administration, navy and temples.
s: Part (a): Cholas and Tanjavur
Part (b): 13th century
Part (c): two features such as administration, navy, temples
Part (d): panel chosen and justified with dates and features

questions.q:
A Chola-era copper plate records a grant of a village to a temple. Its opening lines praise the king and his family in one language, while the later lines, which list the fields and what each family must pay, are in another language. A farmer of the village can read only the second language.
(a) Name the two languages.
(b) Name the Chola capital and the king who founded it as his new capital in the 9th century.
(c) What does the use of both languages show about the Cholas' attitude to literature?
(d) A village panchayat in Tamil Nadu must choose between writing every notice twice, in a formal language and in the local language, which costs more, or writing it once in the formal language only. Using the Chola practice, decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit and Tamil. (b) Tanjavur, made the capital by Vijayalaya. (c) They promoted Tamil as well as Sanskrit literature. (d) A reasoned decision: writing twice costs more but, as in the Chola grants, the operative details reach those affected in the local language while the formal language gives the ceremonial praise; writing once saves money but farmers who cannot read the formal language lose the details.
s: Part (a): Sanskrit and Tamil
Part (b): Tanjavur and Vijayalaya
Part (c): Cholas promoted Tamil as well as Sanskrit
Part (d): decision weighing cost against readers, with the Chola practice

questions.q: What were the subordinate rulers called through whom the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas governed regions they did not rule directly?
questions.a: Samantas, the equivalent of tributaries or vassals. A dvarapandita is a university gatekeeper, a yuvaraja an heir to the throne, and a goshthika a temple's administration council.

questions.q: Which statement about villages in this period is NOT in the chapter?
questions.a: Villages were the lowest administrative units and largely self-governed, overseen by headmen, accountants and local committees. They were not run directly by officers posted from the capital with no local role.
o: Officers from the capital ran villages with no local role
Villages were the lowest administrative units
Headmen and accountants helped oversee them

questions.q: What was one result of the great expansion of the land grant system in this period?
questions.a: A new class of landholders was created; many of them did not till the land themselves. The system did not end private holdings, stop farming or shrink cultivation.
o: A new class of landholders was created
All land passed back to the king
The area under crops fell sharply

questions.q: A vassal chief led the army and managed local administration for his overlord. When the overlord's central authority weakened, the vassal became powerful enough to overthrow him. Which dynasty in the chapter followed this path?
questions.a: The Rashtrakutas, once samantas under the Chalukyas. The Palas were chosen by the people, the Pallavas were overthrown by the Cholas, and the Pratiharas were finally eliminated by the Ghaznavids.

questions.q: A 9th-century inscription in a Tamil village records that a landholder paid for a new tank. What does the chapter say such sponsorship did for the donor?
questions.a: It raised his social status, in addition to helping irrigation. The chapter does not link it with command of the army, tax freedom or becoming a samanta.
o: It put him in command of the army
It freed him from paying any tax
It made him a samanta of the king

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Villages were run directly by officers from the capital, with no role for local people.
2. The Uttaramerur inscriptions of the Cholas detail how the members of the village sabha were selected.
3. The varna-jati system was rigid, and no ruling family ever changed its varna.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. Villages were largely self-governed, and the chapter says varna and jati were flexible, as the Palas and Kakatiyas, originally Shudras, came to be regarded as Kshatriyas.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Indian society in this period remained largely rural and agrarian.
Reason (R): Xuanzang noted the decline of the cities of Kaushambi and Shravasti.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. But the decline of two cities does not explain why society was mainly rural, and the same Xuanzang also described thriving cities like Sthaneshvara, Kanyakubja and Kashi.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each term or name in Column A with Column B.
Column A: 1. Samanta  2. Mandala  3. Kayastha  4. Tribhuvana Mahadevi I
Column B: a. a district  b. a vassal or tributary ruler  c. scribes who became a distinct jati in the 10th century  d. a 9th-century queen of the Bhauma-Karas of present-day Odisha
questions.a: A samanta is a vassal (b); a mandala is a district (a); the Kayasthas, scribes and clerks, became a jati in the 10th century (c); Tribhuvana Mahadevi I was the Bhauma-Kara queen (d). Distractors swap the first two terms, which are both administrative.

questions.q: (a) Name the three levels into which directly controlled territory was divided, from the largest to the smallest. (b) Who oversaw the smallest level?
